crossReferenceObservations.composition: Near asymmetry and enclosing sides frame a broad luminous middle opening.
crossReferenceObservations.terrain: Glacial basins have substantial lateral shoulders and connected drainage; distant ridge angles differ from rounded meadow foreground.
crossReferenceObservations.geology: Rock size hierarchy and orientation connect foreground boulders to bedrock and scree.
crossReferenceObservations.vegetation: Low continuous meadow on gentle slopes, sparse plants on rock, conifer islands at sheltered treeline, flower masses confined to selected patches.
crossReferenceObservations.trees: Tall tapering conifers with branch tiers and irregular gaps; no umbrella crowns.
crossReferenceObservations.palette: Warm meadow light/cool foreground and mountain shadows; saturation and contrast diminish across depth layers.
crossReferenceObservations.atmosphere: Clear foreground, progressively cool/quieter mountain strata; no gray near fog.
crossReferenceObservations.water: Four references use a sinuous small stream as drainage and depth guide; not every archetype needs water.
crossReferenceObservations.frequency: Large slopes and light masses first, medium vegetation/rock clusters second, isolated grass/flower detail last.
crossReferenceObservations.identity: Elevation and glacial geology dominate; lush low plants and narrow conifers distinguish it from savanna.

interpretations: Meadow softness should be expressed by shared pigment fields and restrained curved clumps, not alpine recoloring of gold card bushes.
Tree islands should be field-driven; a fixed ring of identical trees would lose the references natural negative space.
technicalHypotheses: Analytic glacial cross-section plus seeded anisotropic ridge families can generate continuous near/far terrain.
One elevation/slope/aspect/soil/moisture/shelter field should control both palette and placement.
Palette updates should change colors/uniforms, never geology or instance transforms.

directReuse: rock clearance and curved grass shapes

ecologySources.supports: Spruce/fir functional forms, shorter/deformed trees near treeline, shelter-dependent growth.
Treeline is a transition zone rather than a hard boundary.
Strong local gradients in soil moisture and growing season.

scope: Northern Rocky Mountain inspired functional visual study, not verified local species occurrences or surveyed hydrology.
